topic: general Q&A: how applications are read, test-optional, essays, social media
speaker_role: former University of California admissions officer, now college consultant (guest); host is a student/creator
commercial_incentive: Yes: guest is a paid college consultant and the host links her contact details for hiring.
key_insights: Grades and coursework are the core of a review, with essays and activities as supporting pieces when a school requests them.
Between two and four readers may review a file, either individually or in a discussion; if a school asks for an essay, it gets read.
Take test-optional wording at face value: not submitting a score is not treated as a hidden negative, though a score can help with placement or scholarships.
Adversity essays fail when they only name a hardship; readers want what came of it and how it shaped the applicant.
Admissions are conditional: final transcripts are checked in summer, and a large slip in grades or conduct issues can cause trouble, so disclose problems yourself.
Take the most challenging courses you can succeed in and build up gradually rather than piling on honors/AP if it produces poor grades.
Apply to reach schools if you want, but build relationships with reps and balance the list with matches and safeties.
specific_numbers_or_facts: Guest mentions a 350-word essay limit example and stresses staying within word counts.
Guest says some institutions publish GPA/test thresholds for automatic admission or scholarship tiers.
notable_or_distinctive: Mostly generic advice, though the point about conditional admission and self-reporting a grade dip before the final transcript is a useful reminder.
reliability_notes: Dated 2020-era COVID context (class of 2021, test access issues); casual conversation with vague claims and no data.
